read: partial: pp.1-14 (abstract, introduction, related work, benchmark construction, evaluation protocol, experiments, error and difficulty analysis) and pp.20-23 (discussion, limitations, conclusion) read in full; intervention section and appendices (pp.14-20, 23-26) skimmed.
what_it_is: A diagnostic benchmark of closed-form calculations in hypersonic aerodynamics and high-temperature gas dynamics for thermal protection system design, built from Anderson's Hypersonic and High-Temperature Gas Dynamics (pp.1, 4). A five-stage human-AI pipeline (deduplication and OCR repair, rule checks, automated scoring QC, domain-expert review, a three-reviewer go/no-go gate) reduces 4,560 extracted candidates to a 420-item core set in four difficulty levels and eight domains (pp.5-7). Evaluation has two tracks: relative-error bands on the final values with a unit check, and an eight-dimension reasoning rubric scored 0-2 per dimension by a Gemini-3-Pro-Preview judge that sees the reference solution, calibrated against one domain expert on 62 items (weighted kappa 0.68-0.82) (pp.7-10). Twelve models are ranked by the rubric KPI (12.85-87.85), and 11-14% of items for most models are 'right answer, wrong reasoning' (pp.13, 20-21).
domain: engineering: aerospace, hypersonic thermal protection systems (Newtonian theory, shock relations, boundary layers, aerothermal heating, viscous interaction, chemical equilibrium, nonequilibrium flow, radiation; Table IV, p.7)
size: 420 core items (v4; L1 170, L2 120, L3 80, L4 50) and an 810-item pre-gating set (v2), from 4,560 raw candidates (pp.1, 5-7); 12 models in Tables VIII-X plus 6 excluded (pp.10-13), although the text says 13 models
source_of_items: textbook: Anderson, Hypersonic and High-Temperature Gas Dynamics, 2nd ed., via its Chinese translation; extracted by rule-based and LLM passes and repaired by experts (pp.4-6, 22)
has_gold_traces: partial: each item has an expert-confirmed reference solution (checked in Stage 4, p.6) that the rubric judge receives (p.8); no gold intermediate values are checked deterministically
evaluation: final answer plus LLM-judge rubric: Track 1 maps relative error to bands (below 1% = 1.0, 1-10% = 0.7, 10-50% = 0.3, otherwise 0) with a separate unit check, after regex extraction with an LLM fallback (pp.7-9); Track 2 is an eight-dimension weighted rubric (formula selection, parameter identification, unit consistency, calculation accuracy, physical plausibility, assumption justification, result interpretation, presentation clarity) scored 0-2 by a Gemini-3-Pro-Preview judge (pp.8-9); the ranking KPI is the mean rubric score (pp.9-10)
human_validation: Items: Stage 4 domain-expert review of self-containedness, parameter completeness, target definiteness and reference-solution correctness removed 770 of 1,930 candidates; Stage 5 required three reviewers' unanimous go on data quality, evaluation feasibility and reproducibility (p.6). Judge: one domain expert scored 62 items on all eight dimensions; weighted kappa 0.68-0.82 per dimension, 0.75 overall; the judge is more lenient on calculation accuracy (+0.08) and physical plausibility (+0.11); human and judge rankings of six models correlate at Spearman 0.94; 7 items (11%) with a two-point disagreement were adjudicated by a third reviewer (pp.8-10). A 3-item pilot preceded it (p.22).
contamination_measures: none for pretraining contamination (the items come from a published textbook); a chapter-grouped train/development/test split prevents leakage into the fine-tuning interventions (pp.6-7)

engtrace_use.explanation: Not cited in the May paper. Paragraph: engineering (its calibration figures also belong in the judge-validity paragraph). It scores reasoning separately from the answer on engineering calculations and documents right-answer-wrong-reasoning cases (pp.10, 20-21), so the May sentence that existing engineering benchmarks 'remain limited to outcome matching' (May p.3) cannot stand. What EngTrace must say it adds: TPS-CalcBench's process score is a rubric judgment by one LLM, calibrated against a single expert on 62 items (pp.8-10), with no deterministic check of intermediate values; its 420 items are static and come from one public textbook; it covers one aerospace sub-discipline. EngTrace checks code-derived milestones and per-claim arithmetic deterministically, sends only the residue to a judge, and validates that judge against 15 experts across five branches.

suggested_wording: TPS-CalcBench (Zheng et al., 2026) scores reasoning quality separately from numerical accuracy on 420 textbook calculations in hypersonic thermal protection, but its process score is an eight-dimension rubric applied by an LLM judge calibrated against a single expert on 62 items.
facts_to_cite: Analytical (closed-form) calculations in hypersonic aerodynamics and high-temperature gas dynamics, all from Anderson's Hypersonic and High-Temperature Gas Dynamics, 2nd ed. (pp.1, 4).
A five-stage pipeline reduces 4,560 extracted candidates to a 420-item core set (v4) and keeps an 810-item pre-gating set (v2) as a noise control (pp.1, 5-7).
Stage 4 is domain-expert review of self-containedness, parameter completeness, target definiteness and reference-solution correctness; Stage 5 is a three-reviewer go/no-go gate (p.6).
Four difficulty levels L1-L4 with 170, 120, 80 and 50 items, and eight domain categories (Table IV, p.7).

Track 1 scores each target by relative-error band (below 1% = 1.0, 1-10% = 0.7, 10-50% = 0.3, otherwise 0) with a separate unit-correctness check; answers are extracted by regex with an LLM fallback (pp.7-9).

Track 2 scores eight weighted rubric dimensions 0-2 each, from formula selection (weight 0.20) to presentation clarity, by a Gemini-3-Pro-Preview judge given the problem, the reference solution and the model output (pp.8-9).

One domain expert scored 62 items: weighted kappa 0.68-0.82 per dimension (0.75 overall); the judge is more lenient on calculation accuracy (+0.08) and physical plausibility (+0.11); Spearman 0.94 between human and judge rankings of six models (pp.8-10).
The headline KPI is the mean rubric score, so the ranking is judge-based; it runs from 12.85 to 87.85 across 12 models (pp.9-10; Table X, p.13).
For most models, 11-14% of items have an outcome in the exact or acceptable band but a rubric score below 70 ('right answer, wrong reasoning') (pp.20-21).
A calculator tool adds 2.1-2.7 KPI points, concentrated in calculation accuracy (p.11; Table XI, p.14).
The problems are framed in Chinese, from the textbook's Chinese translation (p.22).
overlap_with_engtrace: Shares: engineering calculations with numeric answers and relative-error scoring (pp.7-9); the separation of answer correctness from reasoning quality and the right-answer-wrong-reasoning motivation (pp.1, 20-21), which EngTrace's hard case also measures (correct-answer traces that contain an incorrect step); expert review of items and expert calibration of the judge (pp.6, 8-10); a calculator condition (p.11). Lacks: generated instances (static textbook items, p.4); gold intermediate values or deterministic step checks (the rubric judge also decides calculation accuracy, pp.8-9); multi-expert validation (one expert, 62 items); multi-branch coverage (one aerospace sub-discipline, outside EngTrace's five branches); English problem statements (Chinese framing, p.22).
notes: Paragraph: engineering; also judge validity. (1) Model counts are inconsistent: '13 models from 7 families' (pp.1, 10) with six excluded, yet Tables VIII and X rank 12 models and the text speaks of 'The 12 ranked models' (p.11). (2) The abstract's KPI range 12.6-87.9 differs from Table X's 12.85-87.85 (p.13). (3) The KPI is the rubric score alone, so the headline ranking is judge-based (pp.9-10); outcome bands are reported separately (Table VIII, p.12). (4) The abstract's 'expanded human audit' is one expert on 62 items (p.8). (5) Problems are framed in Chinese (p.22); the revision should not describe it as an English benchmark. The search note's description is otherwise accurate.
